metadata.title: Fantasy Survival Crafting: Inside the Godot Code
metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows
metadata.note: godot-gamedev walker film. Code panels are Godot editor reconstructions with verbatim source; each is followed by real engine output of the same build. No game change, no paid calls, no upload. Vertical companion: designed beats re-rendered as native 9:16 cards or 916 compositions; gameplay re-cut in portrait from the same frames.

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. That's the kind of prompt Walker expects, reconstructed here, not a transcript. This time we open the project itself: a piece of code, then the exact thing it does on screen, in the real build.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a first-person survival-crafting game — wake in an abandoned valley, gather sticks, gold and stone, craft an axe and a campfire, and survive one night until dawn — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: Built: 6 thin scenes, 23 scripts and 3 shaders, 3,303 lines.
Art from Unity asset packs, repaired at load time.

beats.narration_text: Fantasy Survival Crafting is built in code. Its six scene files are a few lines each, and thirty-three hundred lines of GDScript build the whole valley at runtime. So every piece of code we read has a result you can watch.

props.text:
Fantasy Survival Crafting
is built from scenes.
GDScript builds the valley.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Open the game scene and there's one node. Run it, and world dot g d builds the rest: a Level node holding the terrain, the lake, two hundred and sixty-six props, eighty-two pickups, thirty-six pines, nine rabbits and forty-seven grass chunks, then the sky, the sun, and three canvas layers for the HUD, the windows and the menu. Nearly two thousand nodes.

beats.narration_text: The art came from Unity asset packs, and it didn't load cleanly. Every model passes through this function. It repairs the materials, which still point at the original artists' files. For the packs exported from 3ds Max, it rotates the model ninety degrees, so Z-up becomes Y-up.

beats.narration_text: Look is relative mouse motion. While no window is open, each motion event turns the whole body left and right, and tilts only the camera up and down, clamped just short of straight up. The same look function serves the right stick.

beats.narration_text: Selection is a ray from the centre of the screen, four metres long, re-cast every physics frame. If it hits something with a prompt, that becomes the target, and its prompt goes under the crosshair. E or a click acts on that target, and only that.

beats.narration_text: Each recipe row counts what you own. A requirement is green if you have enough, red if not. A recipe that needs a fire also checks the distance. And the Craft button is always created, but it's only visible when every requirement is met.

beats.narration_text: Here's the defect. Each objective line pairs a counter with a done flag. The flag remembers that the axe was crafted. But the counter reads the inventory right now, and crafting just emptied it. So a finished step reads zero of three.

beats.narration_text: A pine counts down its hits. Each chop subtracts one and plays a short shake tween. At zero it falls, and the fall direction is computed from where the player stands, so it always topples away from you.

beats.narration_text: Rabbits port Unity's wandering AI, with one addition. Every physics frame a rabbit checks its distance to the player. Under five metres, it turns directly away and runs at five and a half metres a second, playing its run clip.

beats.narration_text: Drag and drop is Godot's own GUI system. A slot accepts any drop that carries an inventory index, and asks the inventory to move the item, which swaps if the target is full. A right-click on a slot uses the item.

beats.narration_text: Time advances by the frame delta over seconds per hour: twenty-four by day, twelve at night, nine times faster while resting. When night turns to day with a fire placed, a night spent near it, and the player alive, that's victory. Night's arrival posts the warning.

beats.narration_text: Health has two drains here. An empty calorie or water bar costs one health a second. And at night, away from a fire, the cold costs one every one point four seconds. Each hit records its cause, which the defeat screen shows.

beats.narration_text: Saving writes one dictionary: day and hour, the player's position and look, stats, inventory, the equipped tool, flags, counters, removed entities, dropped items, fires and apples. Loading rebuilds the seeded world, then applies that list.

beats.narration_text: The rest of the project, in one pass. A main menu, a three-page story, How to Play, a pause menu and two end screens. Three shaders for terrain, water and sky. An audio autoload of synthesized sounds. And a tools folder with two playtests that pass forty-two checks, by calling game functions directly. The film's captures pressed the keys instead.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This is a project you can read top to bottom: thin scenes, one world script that builds everything, a repair layer for the asset packs, and a save that lists exactly what changed. One display bug: ticked objectives that read zero of three. Its own tests call functions; the captures pressed keys. And nobody has played it yet.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude in your own Godot project: Use Walker on my Godot project. Find one place where the screen shows state from two different sources, like a counter and a done flag, and predict a moment when they disagree. Then write a capture that proves or disproves it with real input, and only after that, propose the smallest code change. Liam, in for Bear.
